messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame was forty-six years old, a park ranger in a sprawling national forest in the Pacific Northwest, a job he had taken after two decades in the military. He had served as a combat medic in a prolonged deployment in a dense, humid region where the air was thick with rot and diesel. The event that had fractured him occurred during a routine supply convoy. An IED detonated beneath the lead vehicle, and in the ensuing chaos, a helicopter had been called in for a medevac. Kwame had worked on three men, two of whom did not survive. For years after, he had managed, but then the sounds of the forest began to betray him. A distant aircraft, even a commercial plane, would cause his stomach to drop. The crack of a dry branch under a hiker’s boot would make him freeze. He had come to believe that these sounds were not just noises but signals, warnings that he was about to be ambushed again.

What frightened Kwame most was the way his own mind seemed to have turned against him. When he heard a helicopter—and he heard them often, as they flew over the park for fire patrols or rescue missions—he did not simply feel startled. He felt a surge of threat so immediate and physical that he would drop into a crouch, scanning the treeline for muzzle flashes. The sound triggered a cascade: he would then become convinced that he had to be on guard all the time, that he had permanently changed for the worse, and that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what had happened. In those moments, his memories of the event felt more real and vivid than the trail in front of him. He could smell the thick, oily smoke and the sickly-sweet scent of blood, as though he were still kneeling in the mud beside the burning vehicle.

The memory itself reinforced his negative appraisals. Every time he recalled the event with that unbearable clarity—the way the images were sharper than the present—he would think, *I have permanently changed for the worse.* This thought would then make him more sensitive to triggers. He began to watch other people closely for signs that they might harm him, even the families picnicking by the lake. He would scan the parking lots for anything out of place, his heart rate climbing before he had even identified a threat. The hypervigilance was exhausting, but he was certain that letting his guard down would lead to disaster. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that he was the only one who could keep himself safe, even though he also believed he was broken beyond repair.

The cycle tightened over the months. A trigger—say, the distant thrum of rotor blades—would spike his threat level, and that state of high alert would drag the memory back into his mind with full sensory force. Then the memory would confirm his negative self-view, which in turn made him more reactive to the next sound. He avoided the busier parts of the park, rerouting his patrols to areas where aircraft were less common. His wife noticed he no longer wanted to go to the grocery store, because the hum of the refrigerators reminded him of the engine of the helicopter. He had begun to feel detached, unreal, as though he were watching his own life from a great distance.

It was his wife who finally insisted he seek help, after he had spent an entire afternoon hiding in the maintenance shed because a search-and-rescue helicopter had been circling for hours. Kwame sat in the clinic, his hands resting on his knees, and said that what he was most afraid of was that he would never feel normal again, that the permanent damage was already done, and that he was only going through the motions of a life he no longer believed he deserved.
